q.intro.text: A sensor logs a quantity y once a second: two, four, eight, fourteen, twenty two. Linear, quadratic or exponential? Pick one, and say how sure you are.

e.intro.text: Three tests, after one check. Press each step. The table changes first, then the notation.

e.step0.text: First the inputs. Every x step is plus one. Equal steps, so differences and ratios compare equal intervals. Without that, no test means anything.

e.step1.text: Ratios of neighbours: times two, times two, then times one point seven five, and about times one point five seven. The doubling stops after two steps, so the table is not exponential. A factor has to hold on every step.

e.step2.text: First differences: plus two, plus four, plus six, plus eight. Not equal, so it is not linear either. But look: they grow by the same amount each time.

e.step3.text: Second differences: plus two, plus two, plus two. Constant, and not zero. The table is consistent with a quadratic function. In fact, y equals x squared plus x plus two fits every row.

e.why.text: Quick check: why did the doubling in the first rows not prove exponential?

e.why.ok.text: Yes. A family test is about every pair of neighbouring rows. Two equal ratios are a start, not a pattern. The third one breaks it.

e.why.even.text: Even numbers have nothing to do with it. Fourteen divided by eight is one point seven five, not two. The factor changes.

e.why.start.text: Exponential tables can start anywhere. The problem is that the ratio does not stay the same.

t.intro.text: Your turn, with all three tests. A new table: x is zero, two, four, six, eight, and y is three, six, twelve, twenty four, forty eight.

t.step.text: Check the inputs first. Which is true?

t.step.ok.text: Right. Every x step is plus two. Equal steps of any size are fine.

t.step.one.text: The steps do not have to be plus one. They have to be equal, and these are all plus two.

t.step.uneq.text: Subtract neighbours. Two minus zero, four minus two, and so on. All plus two: equal.

t.d1.text: Type the first difference from x equals two to x equals four.

t.d1.ok.text: Yes. Twelve minus six is six. The first differences are plus three, plus six, plus twelve, plus twenty four. Not equal, so not linear.

t.d1.ratio.text: That is the ratio, twelve divided by six. A difference subtracts: twelve minus six.

t.d1.other.text: Subtract the y values: the one at x equals four, minus the one at x equals two.

t.quad.text: The first differences keep changing. Is the table quadratic, then?

t.quad.ok.text: Right. Check before you claim. Second differences: plus three, plus six, plus twelve. Not constant: not quadratic.

t.quad.no.text: Changing first differences only rule out linear. Exponential tables have them too. The second differences decide: plus three, plus six, plus twelve.

t.ratio.text: Last test. Type the ratio of neighbours, twelve divided by six.

t.ratio.ok.text: Yes, times two. And six over three, twenty four over twelve, forty eight over twenty four are times two too. Every ratio is the same.

t.ratio.diff.text: Six is the difference. The ratio divides: twelve divided by six.

t.ratio.other.text: Divide the later value by the earlier one: twelve divided by six.

t.fam.text: So what is the table consistent with?

t.fam.ok.text: Right. Exponential, times two for every step of two in x. Per single unit of x, the factor is smaller: it takes two units to double.

t.fam.unit.text: The x steps are plus two, so times two is the factor per step of two, not per one unit of x.

t.fam.quad.text: The second differences were plus three, plus six, plus twelve: not constant. The ratios are the test that passes.

q.cb.right.text: At the start you picked quadratic, and the tests agree: constant second differences of plus two.

q.cb.exp.text: At the start you picked exponential. The first rows double, but the ratio test fails at fourteen over eight. A test must hold on every step.

q.cb.lin.text: At the start you picked linear. The first differences are plus two, plus four, plus six, plus eight: not equal. The second differences settle it: quadratic.

q.cb.none.text: Check equal x steps, then first differences, second differences and ratios. One test, or none, passes on every step.

p.intro.text: Sam’s table of f of x has first differences plus three, plus three, plus three, plus three. So the rule is linear, proved, says Sam. Is it?

p.test.text: Look at g. It agrees with the line on all five rows, and at x equals five it gives forty six, not sixteen. A table is only consistent with a family.

p.build.text: Right. A table is only consistent with a family. What is always true goes the other way: every linear function gives equal differences. Prove it. Fill each because.

p.build2.text: Now the direction that is always true: every linear function gives equal differences. Prove it. Fill each because.

p.c1.text: Right. f of x plus h means: the rule, with x plus h in place of x.

p.c2.text: Right. m times x plus h is m x plus m h. The m x and the c cancel, leaving m h.

p.c3.text: Right. m h has no x in it, so it is the same wherever the step starts.

p.no.examples.text: That is Sam’s argument. Rows are examples. The claim is about every x.

p.no.shift.text: f of x plus h is the rule with x plus h put in, not f of x, plus h.

p.no.converse.text: That is the other direction, and g just showed it is false.

p.no.other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line. Which reason makes this line true?

p.done.text: Proved. A linear function gives the same difference, m h, for every step of size h. A table can only show consistency. The rule guarantees the pattern.
